abstract.text:
Abstract—With the development of large-scale renewable energy
sources (RESs) and voltage source converter-based high voltage
direct current (VSC-HVDC) technologies, integrating RESs into
power systems through VSC-HVDC systems has become
increasingly popular. The four-quadrant power control
characteristics of VSC converters enable them to function as
flexible reactive power sources, which help alleviate voltage
stability issues in power systems. However, the implicit functional
relationship between the reactive power limits of VSC converters
and their output active power, as well as the nonlinear DC power
flow between VSC converters in a multi-terminal VSC-HVDC
system, make the reactive power boundary of each VSC
converter a nonlinear dynamic variable. This adds further
complexity to calculating the static voltage stability region
boundary (SVSRB). In this paper, an approximate computation
model for the SVSR of power systems integrated with large-scale
RESs through VSC-HVDC systems is proposed, considering the
influences of DC network topology, DC control strategies, control
parameters, and other factors. The SVSR is displayed from the
perspective of RESs, which helps intuitively evaluate the
influence of the DC integration system on the SVSR.

introduction.text:
I. I NTRODUCTION
With the development of power electronic technologies,
voltage source converter-based high voltage direct current
(VSC-HVDC) transmission has attracted widespread attention
for integrating large-scale, remote renewable energy sources
(RES). However, the increasing penetration level of renewable
energy introduces significant volatility and randomness from
large-scale RESs, which has a non-negligible impact on the
static voltage stability (SVS) of power systems and can lead to
voltage instability [1]. Therefore, evaluating the voltage
stability margin (VSM) and preventing the system from
voltage collapse have become critical areas of focus for
researchers.
A static voltage stability region (SVSR) is a subset of a
security region with respect to the active power injection
satisfying the voltage stability [2] And the space between the
operating point of the system and the SVSR boundary
(SVSRB) demonstrates the VSM with respect to a given stress
direction [3]. Mathematically, the SVSR is a hyper-surface in
parameter space, providing an effective solution to stress
direction deviation problems caused by the fluctuating RESs .
Existing studies on SVSR are primarily based on pure AC
systems [4-5], while research on SVSR considering the
integration of RESs with VSC-HVDC systems remains largely
unexplored.
The integration of RES into power systems with HVDC
systems typically represents them as large power plants,
whose capacity is comparable to that of conventional coal-
fired power plants. Due to the four-quadrant power control
capability of VSC converters, each terminal can continuously
and independently control active and reactive power. VSC
converters can provide excellent reactive power regulation to
the AC system. The work in [6-7] depicted the reactive power
boundaries of VSC converters, revealing the complex
coupling relationships between the reactive power limits of
VSC converters and their output active power. When the DC
system is a multi-terminal VSC-HVDC (MTDC) system, the
situation becomes more complicated. Due to the connections
within the DC network, the active power of each terminal is
coupled with others and fluctuates with the RESs. As a result,
the reactive power boundary of each VSC converter on the AC
system side becomes a nonlinear dynamic variable. The
nonlinear dynamic characteristics of the converter reactive
power limits further complicate the construction of the static
voltage stability region boundary (SVSRB) of the power
system. Moreover, to ensure the accuracy of the SVSRB,
multiple AC/DC power flow calculations are required to
determine the convergence of power flow and to obtain
multiple saddle-node bifurcation (SNB) points. This poses a
significant challenge of high computational complexity when
building the SVSRB using traditional sampling-fitting
methods.
In this paper, an approximate computation model for
SVSR of the power system integrated with large-scaled RESs
by VSC-HVDC system is presented. Firstly, a linearized DC
power flow model, considering different DC control strategies,

is developed to obtain the analytical expressions of the active
power at the AC system side of the HVDC terminals with
respect to variations in RESs. Secondly, an approach
searching for dynamic converter reactive power constraints is
presented, considering the parameters of the VSC converters
and the DC power flow restrictions in the DC network. And
then an approximate computation model of SVSR of the
power system is developed using the method of PV curves.
SVSR of the AC system is depicted from the perspective of
RESs for the first time, which helps to evaluate the
corresponding Voltage Stability Margin (VSM) of injecting
RES power and ensures that the system operates within the
SVSR, leveraging the flexible controllability of the VSC-
HVDC system.

conclusion.text:
Ⅲ. CONCLUSION
In this paper, an approach for developing an approximate
computation model of SVSR considering the integration of
large-scale RESs through a VSC-HVDC system is proposed.
The characteristics of the VSC-HVDC system, including the
DC network, DC control strategy, and control parameters, are
considered in the modeling of SVSR for the first time. The
high precision and fast calculation speed of the method are
also demonstrated.
The proposed approach displays the SVSR from the
perspective of RESs instead of the PCCs in the power system.
This allows for an intuitive evaluation of the corresponding
VSM when injecting RES power and ensures that the
operation of RESs remains within the SVSR, leveraging the
flexible control capabilities of the VSC-HVDC system to their
fullest extent.
